verdict.rationale: The service word-group is applied to named women densely and across multiple books. Phoebe is ousan diakonon (G1249) of the church at Cenchreae and a prostatis of many (Rom 16:1-2); the same diakon- root in its verb form diakoneo (G1247) describes the women who ministered to Jesus out of their means in Luke 8:3, Mark 15:41, and Matt 27:55, and the noun diakonia (G1248) names the mercy and relief service of Acts 6:1 and 2 Cor 8-9. Prisca is a synergos (G4904, fellow worker), Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, and Persis kopiao (G2872, labored hard) in the Lord, Euodia and Syntyche struggled alongside Paul in the gospel, Tabitha is full of good works and almsgiving (eleemosyne, G1654, Acts 9:36), and older women are kalodidaskaloi (Titus 2:3) teaching younger women. The vocabulary uniformly and repeatedly attaches significant serving, mercy, patronage, gospel-labor, and women-to-women instruction to women, which is exactly the non-authoritative scope the proposition claims. The one lexically contested datum, whether diakonos in Rom 16:1 and the gynaikas hosautos of 1 Tim 3:11 denote a recognized deacon office, bears on office and authority, not on the serving roles in view, so the affirmation stands with high confidence.

scripture.force: Phoebe is commended (synistemi, G4921) as ousan diakonon (present participle of eimi plus diakonos, G1249) of the church at Cenchreae and named adelphe (G0079, sister). The lexeme diakonos is common in grammatical gender, takes no feminine ending here, and is the same word used of male ministers and of the deacon context in 1 Timothy 3, so it plainly marks her as a recognized servant of a named local assembly while leaving the office-versus-function question open.

Phoebe is described as a prostatis (G4368, a patron, protector, or helper) of many including Paul himself, with the congregation urged to receive her axios ton hagion (worthily of the saints) and to assist her. The noun prostatis is a hapax legomenon, occurring only here in the canon, so its precise force, ranging from material patron to one who stands before, cannot be triangulated from other uses, but every reading places a substantial supportive ministry by a woman toward many.

Prisca and Aquila are jointly called tous synergous mou en Christo Iesou (G4904, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus). The woman Prisca is grouped under the same labor noun Paul applies to his male coworkers (the same term recurs of Urbanus in Rom 16:9 and of Timothy and others), with no gendered qualification of the word.

Mary is described with the feminine relative hetis and the aorist ekopiasen polla (from kopiao, G2872) eis hymas, that she labored much for the recipients. Kopiao is the same strenuous-labor verb Paul uses of his own gospel toil in 1 Cor 15:10 and of elders who labor in 1 Tim 5:17, applied here to a woman's work for the church.

Andronicus and the personal name Iounia (G2458, stored under one Strong for both the feminine Junia and the rare masculine Junias) are episemoi en tois apostolois (G1978 plus G0652, well known among or to the apostles). The gender of the name and the sense of episemoi en, prominent among versus well known to, are both genuinely contested at the lexical level, so this verse is treated as complicating rather than as load-bearing for the verdict.

Tryphaena and Tryphosa are tas kopiosas en kyrio (the women laboring in the Lord) and Persis the agapeten (beloved, G0027) ekopiasen polla en kyrio. The participial and aorist forms of kopiao (G2872) are applied to three named women, presenting sustained ministry labor as their characteristic activity.

Joanna, Susanna, and many other women diekonoun (imperfect of diakoneo, G1247) to Jesus and the Twelve ek ton hyparchonton autais, out of their own means. The same diakon- root that names Phoebe as diakonos here describes ongoing material and supportive service rendered by named women, the verb being the broad render-service term used pan-canonically.

Tabitha (Dorcas) is pleres ergon agathon kai eleemosynon (full of good works, agathos G0018, and almsgivings, eleemosyne G1654) which she was doing. The mercy and good-works vocabulary frames a woman's sustained diaconal and charitable ministry, the very category of serving and mercy role the proposition names.

Priscilla and Aquila together proselabonto (took aside) Apollos and exethento (expounded) to him the way of God more accurately (akribesteron). The plural verbs take both as subjects, with the woman Priscilla often named first, describing private instruction of a man in a non-assembly, non-pulpit setting.

Paul names Euodia and Syntyche, two women, and parakalo (G3870, urges) each by name to be of the same mind in the Lord. They are addressed as significant individuals within the congregation whose unity Paul considers worth a direct apostolic appeal.

The two women are aitines (feminine relative) who synethlesan (struggled alongside) Paul en to euangelio (in the gospel) together with Clement and the rest of his synergon (G4904, fellow workers), their names en biblo zoes (in the book of life). The athletic compound verb places their gospel labor alongside Paul's male coworkers.

Older women (presbytidas) are directed to be hieroprepeis (reverent), not diabolous (slanderers) nor enslaved to much wine, and to be kalodidaskalous (G2567, teachers of good). The compound noun kalodidaskalos is a hapax legomenon, occurring only here, so its scope is fixed entirely by its immediate context, which the next verse directs toward instruction of younger women.

The purpose clause hina sophronizosi tas neas (that they may train the young women) defines the scope of the older women's teaching as instruction of younger women in loving husbands and children. The lexical frame places this ministry within a woman-to-woman, household-oriented setting.

The instruction lists younger women being sophronas, hagnas, agathas (good, G0018), and managing the household, hina me ho logos tou theou blasphemetai (G0987, that the word of God not be blasphemed). The clause assumes ongoing intra-female instruction as a normal and commended ministry, while hypotassomenas tois idiois andrasin bounds it within household order.

complicating_texts.resolution: Within the deacon-qualification section bounded by diakonos (G1249) at verses 8 and 12, verse 11 reads gynaikas hosautos (women likewise) using the same connector hosautos (G5615) that introduced the deacons at verse 8. The noun gynaikas is anarthrous and carries no possessive pronoun, so it can read as women deacons or as deacons wives, and the grammar does not disambiguate. This ambiguity concerns whether a recognized deacon office included women, which is an office and authority question. The proposition restricts itself to non-authoritative serving roles, which the broader diakon- vocabulary establishes regardless of how verse 11 is resolved, so the unresolved grammar does not unsettle the verdict on the practice as stated.

The personal name Iounia (G2458) and the phrase episemoi en tois apostolois carry both a gender question (Junia feminine versus the rare Junias masculine) and a sense question (well known to the apostles versus prominent among the apostles). These bear on whether a woman held apostolic standing, which touches authoritative office, not the non-authoritative serving roles in view. The verdict does not rest on this verse, so its ambiguity does not weaken the affirmation of diaconal, mercy, and helping ministry.

variant_units_examined.note: The accentuation and reading of the name Iounian (feminine Junia versus rare masculine Junias) bears on whether a woman is in view among or known to the apostles, but the verdict for non-authoritative serving roles does not depend on this name or on apostolic standing.

variants.note: All anchor verses are New Testament and outside the ingested 3 John CBGM window, so apparatus examination is in shadow status. The named-woman service vocabulary (diakonos, diakoneo, synergos, kopiao, eleemosyne) is textually stable across the relevant witnesses for the verses cited.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the diakonos, diakoneo, synergos, kopiao, and eleemosyne vocabulary applied to Phoebe, the ministering women of Luke 8, Tabitha, Mary, and the Philippian women as commending women in mercy, hospitality, patronage, gospel-labor, and women-to-women instruction precisely because the proposition limits these to non-authoritative settings, keeping recognized eldership and assembly teaching authority a separate question that texts like 1 Tim 2 and the office-side of 1 Tim 3 govern.

Reads the same diakonos applied to Phoebe of a named church, the gynaikas hosautos of 1 Tim 3:11 as women deacons, and episemoi en tois apostolois of Junia, as evidence that women held recognized ministry standing without the non-authoritative limitation, and so affirms the practice as stated and would extend the same vocabulary further into office.

hermeneutics.notes: Both readings affirm the proposition as stated. They diverge only on whether the very same diakon- and apostolic vocabulary also licenses recognized office, which the non-authoritative qualifier of this proposition deliberately leaves outside its scope. The divergence is a matter of how far the words reach, not whether women served.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Women in the New Testament are associated with serving, mercy, hospitality, evangelism, helping, and instruction-of-women functions; the question is whether the lexical pattern shows such roles being exercised by women apart from recognized assembly teaching or governing authority.
stem_audit.notes: The phrases non-authoritative contexts and gifting and calling are not gender-restricted presuppose a prior office-versus-non-office boundary that itself reflects a particular reading. The verdict is derived on the original stem, but the neutralized form removes the embedded boundary so the lexical observation about women laboring in these capacities is assessed on its own terms. Affirms is unchanged from the prior file; the enrichment added the diakon- verb and noun (G1247, G1248), the prostatis and kalodidaskalos hapax data, and the Luke 8:3 and Acts 9:36 corroborating texts, and relocated the central ambiguity to 1 Tim 3:11.

lay_summary: When Paul closes his letter to the Romans he names many women and says what they actually did. Phoebe is called a diakonos, a servant, of the church at Cenchreae, and a prostatis, a patron or helper, of many people including Paul. Prisca is called a fellow worker in Christ Jesus, the same word Paul uses for his male coworkers. Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, and Persis are each said to have labored hard in the Lord, using a strong word for toil. The verb form of the same servant word describes the women in Luke 8 who ministered to Jesus out of their own means, and in Acts a woman named Tabitha is full of good works and almsgiving. In Philippians, Euodia and Syntyche struggled alongside Paul in the gospel. In Acts, Priscilla joins her husband in privately explaining the way of God to Apollos. In Titus, older women are to be teachers of good things who train the younger women. Read together, the Greek vocabulary for serving, mercy, patronage, gospel-labor, and women-to-women teaching is attached to women again and again and is commended. The proposition limits these to non-authoritative settings, apart from assembly governing or pulpit authority, and within that limit the words straightforwardly support it. Two points are genuinely disputed, but both touch the separate office question, not the serving roles. In 1 Timothy 3, in the middle of the list of qualifications for deacons, the phrase women likewise has no possessive, so it can mean women deacons or deacons wives, and the grammar does not settle it. In Romans 16:7 a person named Junia is notable among or to the apostles, and both the name and the phrase are contested. Because the affirmation rests on the broad serving vocabulary and not on these two contested verses, the conclusion is that the lexical evidence affirms the practice as stated, with high confidence on the serving roles themselves and an honest note that any extension to formal office is where the same words are argued.
